subject: political-science
lectureTitle: Lecture 1: Introduction to Power, Politics and Political Science (MDJ)

cards.front: What is **politics** in OD's sense, and what makes that definition **procedural**?
cards.back: The **process by which human communities make collective decisions** at any scale. It is **procedural** because it concerns **how** decisions get made, not **what** they contain.

Procedural: politics is the **process** of making collective decisions. Distributional: politics is a **game of allocating resources**, deciding who wins and who loses (Lasswell: "who gets what, when, how"; Easton: "the authoritative allocation of values"). The distributional view rests on **scarcity** and **preference heterogeneity**.

cards.front: Compare the **three faces of power** (Dahl · Bachrach & Baratz · Lukes).
cards.back: 1) **First, decision making (Dahl):** winning an **observable** conflict. 2) **Second, agenda setting (Bachrach & Baratz):** keeping issues **off the agenda** through non decisions. 3) **Third, ideological (Lukes):** shaping what people **want**, with no visible conflict. Power grows **less visible** going down.
cards.hint: Win it → block it → prevent the wish.

cards.front: Whose framework sets out the **three dimensions of power**?
cards.back: **Lukes (1974).** He built on **Dahl (1957)** and **Bachrach & Baratz (1962)** to add the third, ideological dimension.

cards.front: "What explains political behaviour?" splits into which **three answer families**?
cards.back: **Interests** (actors pursue their own preferences), **Beliefs** (values and ideas), and **Structures** (broad forces shape and limit behaviour).

Pluralist: power is **dispersed** among many competing groups, none winning permanently (Dahl); it works mostly in the **first** face. Elite: a **small elite** controls almost all power (Mills, Winters), using the **second and third** faces.

cards.front: What is **political economy** as a method (Ansell)?
cards.back: Modelling each person as a **self interested utility maximizer**, then scaling up to watch collective goals **undermined by us**. It begins from individuals (**methodological individualism**).
When **self interested individuals interacting** inadvertently **undermine a shared goal**. Each choice is individually rational yet collectively ruinous.

cards.front: Name the concept: an **unowned shared resource** gets over exploited because no one can be excluded.
cards.back: The **tragedy of the commons.** Each user's extra take imposes a **negative externality** on everyone else.

Institutions are **formal rules or organizations** that lock in expectations (e.g. the filibuster). Norms are **informal expectations** about how we should behave: powerful but vaguer and harder to enforce. Both make a political promise **self enforcing**.

cards.front: Run **Ansell's chain** explaining why politics fails, in order.
cards.back: 1) **Self interest.** 2) **Collective action problem** (we are interdependent). 3) **Tragedy of the commons** or externality. 4) Need for a **political promise**. 5) **Institutions and norms** make the promise self enforcing.
